items.title: fix(benchmark): capture warmup end time before benchmark phase
items.body:
## Bug
Warmup duration in benchmark results was incorrect. It showed ~5500 ms for `--benchmark-fast` (500ms warmup + 5000ms benchmark + processing). The reported warmup time included the entire benchmark phase.

## Root cause
`warmup_duration_ms` was calculated as:
```c
result->warmup_duration_ms = (int)(get_microseconds() - warmup_start) / 1000;
```
But `get_microseconds()` was called at line 156, **after** the benchmark phase completed. So it captured warmup + benchmark + result processing time.

## Fix
Capture `warmup_end = get_microseconds()` immediately after the warmup loop ends (line 110), before the benchmark phase starts. Use `warmup_end - warmup_start` for the warmup duration report.

## Before/After
| | Warmup reported | Actual warmup |
|---|---|---|
| Before | ~5501 ms | 500 ms |
| After | 500 ms | 500 ms |

**Do not merge without explicit approval.**

items.title: fix(interp): make recursive trace boundary explicit
items.body:
## Summary

Fixes #184.

The Fannkuch compare benchmark could produce incorrect results in `default` and `jit` modes while `threaded` remained correct.

## Root cause

The trace recorder used `skipCall` when it encountered a recursive `CALL`. That is only sound when the recorder can model the call's effects. `skipCall` supplies placeholder return values and does not reproduce the callee's heap mutations.

A recursive call encountered inside a non-entry loop trace could therefore leave the recorder with a speculative VM/heap state that never existed. Fannkuch exposes this because its recursive permutation routine mutates a shared array and continues execution after the call.

## Fix

Treat recursive calls in non-entry loop traces as a trace boundary. The native prefix is retained, the real recursive call executes through the threaded path, and the post-call continuation can be captured from the actual frame and heap state.

Function-entry self-recursion keeps the existing native `selfCall` path, so the fix does not disable native recursive-call lowering globally or reject heap mutation from JIT plans.

The JIT trace contract documentation is updated to describe the boundary explicitly.

## Validation

- `go test -race ./...`
- `go vet ./...`
- `go test -tags=compare -run='^$' -bench='^BenchmarkCall_Fannkuch$' -benchtime=1x -count=5`
- `git diff --check`

The Fannkuch compare benchmark passes for `default`, `threaded`, `jit`, `native`, `gpython`, and `cpython` on the ARM64 development machine.

items.title: eval: harden OpenSRE LLM judge JSON extraction
items.body:
## Summary

This PR improves the robustness of the OpenSRE evaluation pipeline by hardening how LLM judge responses are parsed and validated.

The current evaluation flow relies on extracting a JSON object from LLM outputs. However, real LLM responses are often not strictly well-formed and may include additional text, markdown fences, or malformed structures. This can lead to unstable or incorrect benchmark results.

## Problem

The existing `extract_judge_json_from_response` implementation:

- assumes a clean JSON object in the response
- does not explicitly reject JSON arrays
- can incorrectly extract partial JSON from mixed outputs
- is not tested against real-world LLM response patterns

As a result, evaluation can silently succeed with incorrect parsing or fail unpredictably depending on LLM formatting.

## Changes

- Hardened JSON extraction logic:
  - captures full fenced content (not just `{...}`) to avoid partial extraction
  - explicitly rejects JSON arrays (`[...]`), including fenced cases
  - improves detection of valid JSON object boundaries
  - ensures only dictionary outputs are accepted

- Added dedicated test coverage for judge parsing:
  - clean JSON responses
  - markdown fenced JSON (```json)
  - mixed prose + JSON outputs
  - missing JSON cases
  - JSON arrays (invalid)
  - malformed JSON
  - fenced JSON arrays (invalid, now explicitly rejected)

## Why this matters

OpenSRE evaluation depends on LLM judge outputs for scoring (`overall_pass`, `score_0_100`, etc.).

This change improves:

- evaluation stability
- reproducibility of benchmark results
- robustness to real LLM output variability
- prevents silent mis-scoring due to partial JSON extraction

items.title: Fix Microsoft Graph request failures in CIS Benchmark and sync_o365_data
items.body:
Two bugs caused Graph API calls to silently fail or produce incorrect benchmark results in tenants with paginated policy lists.

## Root causes

### 1. Generic error message broke 403 detection
`_graph_get` raised `M365Error("Microsoft Graph request failed")` without the HTTP status code. `_check_audit_log_enabled` checks `"403" in str(exc)` to distinguish Forbidden (→ `FAIL`) from other errors (→ `UNKNOWN`) — this check never matched.

```python
# Before
raise M365Error("Microsoft Graph request failed")

# After
raise M365Error(f"Microsoft Graph request failed ({response.status_code})")
```

### 2. Benchmark checks fetched only first page of policy collections
`conditionalAccessPolicies` and `deviceCompliancePolicies` are paginated. All three CA policy checks (`_check_legacy_auth_blocked`, `_check_mfa_conditional_access`, `_check_admin_mfa`) and all three Intune runners called `_graph_get` once and discarded `@odata.nextLink`. A blocking policy on page 2 would cause a false FAIL.

## Changes

- **`app/services/m365.py`** — HTTP status code in `_graph_get` error message; add `_graph_get_all` pagination helper
- **`app/services/cis_benchmark.py`** — add local `_graph_get_all` (uses module-level `_graph_get` so existing test mocks still intercept paginated calls); replace single-page `_graph_get` calls with `_graph_get_all` for all collection endpoints
- **`tests/test_cis_benchmark.py`** — 5 new tests: status code in error, 403→`FAIL`/500→`UNKNOWN` audit-log detection, pagination follows `@odata.nextLink`, CA policy check passes when blocking policy is on page 2

items.title: Fix three correctness bugs: missing data module, wrong EO gap for single groups, sensitive attribute leaking into training features
items.body:
Three bugs that produce incorrect benchmark results, ranging from a crash-on-import to silently wrong fairness metrics.

## Fixes

### 🔴 Missing `src/benchmark/data.py` (crash)
A modularization commit deleted `data.py` but never created the replacement `data/` package. `runner.py` still imports `load_folktables`, `load_folktables_by_period`, and `stratified_split` from it → `ModuleNotFoundError` on startup. Recreated the module with all required functions plus the `keep_sensitive_cols` parameter expected by the current runner.

### 🔴 Static mode: sensitive attribute leaked into training features
`load_folktables(..., keep_sensitive_cols=True)` was passed in static mode without the subsequent `reindex(columns=base_columns)` that temporal mode uses to strip the primary attribute. The model received SEX as a training feature and exploited it directly:

```
DP Gap WITH sensitive attribute in features (bug): 0.477
DP Gap WITHOUT sensitive attribute (correct):      0.067
```

7× inflation of the fairness gap; method comparisons were meaningless. Fixed by removing `keep_sensitive_cols=True` from the static-mode load call (default `False`), matching temporal-mode behaviour.

### 🟡 `equalized_odds_gap` returned wrong non-NaN for single-group subsets
When `_compute_stratified_metrics` evaluated per-subgroup metrics (e.g. all samples with `A=1`), `equalized_odds_gap` computed the absent group's TPR/FPR as `0.0` fallback and returned that as if it were a real gap. Fixed with an early-return `np.nan` when either group is absent — consistent with `demographic_parity` and `observed_expected_gap`.

### 🟡 `np.mean` → `np.nanmean` in temporal metric aggregation
All three temporal aggregation loops used `np.mean`, so a single `NaN` period (e.g. from the single-group fix above) propagated to the final aggregated result. Changed to `np.nanmean`.

### 🟢 Dead code removed
Lines computing `metrics_race`/`result_entry_race` on the full aggregated temporal test set were guarded by `if mode != "temporal"` inside `if mode == "temporal"` — always `False`. The results were silently discarded while wasting a full `compute_metrics()` pass over millions of rows. Block removed; per-year race metrics are correctly handled in the per-year loop.

### 🟢 `data.py` quality improvements
Extracted the duplicated `(y*2 + A)` strata encoding into `_create_strata()` helper; replaced `np.isclose` split-ratio guard with `abs(sum - 1.0) > 1e-9`.

items.body:
## Summary

This PR fixes multiple critical bugs across the CXR grounding benchmark that caused silent failures, incorrect results, and crashes. The changes include:

1. **Extraction of shared utilities** into a new `cxr_common.py` module to eliminate code duplication and fix bugs in image loading and box parsing
2. **Critical box parsing fixes** that were causing complete detection failures for some models
3. **Coordinate handling improvements** including proper clamping and tolerance for floating-point rounding
4. **Model-specific inference fixes** for RadVLM, CheXagent, MAIRA-2, and BioViL-T
5. **HPC deployment infrastructure** with setup scripts and job templates

## Key Changes

### Core Fixes in `cxr_common.py` (new file)

- **Normalized-scale box detection** (HIGH IMPACT): Changed from all-or-nothing `all(0.0 <= v <= 1.0)` check to a `-0.05 <= v <= 1.05` tolerance band with per-coordinate clamping. This fixes a real bug where boxes like `[0.1, 0.2, 1.02, 0.95]` (plausible float-rounding artifacts) would fail detection entirely and be misinterpreted as raw pixel coordinates, producing degenerate 1×1 boxes.

- **Removed unreachable 0-1000 scale heuristic**: The condition `max(vals) > img_w and max(vals) > img_h` could never fire correctly for MIMIC-CXR images (2000-3000px), making this dead code that would misinterpret coordinates if it ever did execute.

- **Added coordinate clamping**: Boxes straddling image edges are now clamped to `[0, img_w] × [0, img_h]` before returning, preventing out-of-range coordinates from reaching downstream consumers.

- **Guarded `box_iou()` against degenerate boxes**: Now explicitly returns `0.0` if either box has area ≤ 0, preventing nonsensical IoU values.

- **Multi-frame color DICOM support**: Added explicit handling for 4D pixel arrays `(frames, H, W, samples)` before the grayscale multi-frame check.

- **Unified image loader**: Consolidated six duplicate implementations with improved DICOM handling (RescaleSlope/Intercept, VOI LUT, MONOCHROME1 inversion, truncated JPEG tolerance).

- **RadVLM** (`radvlm_medsam.py`):

items.title: Implement bytecode VM compiler for KL functions
items.body:
## Summary

This PR implements a bytecode VM compiler for KL functions, replacing the tree-walking interpreter for `defun` bodies. The compiler translates KL forms to a flat instruction sequence with indexed local variables, eliminating the O(depth) environment lookups and per-call heap allocations that were the primary performance bottleneck.

## Key Changes

- **New bytecode compiler** (`kl/compiler.go`): Compiles KL expressions to a stack-based instruction set with support for:
  - Special forms: `defun`, `lambda`, `freeze`, `let`, `if`, `cond`, `and`, `or`, `do`, `type`, `trap-error`
  - Function calls with tail-call optimization and self-tail-call trampolining
  - Closure capture via upvalue discovery during compilation
  - Arithmetic fast-paths for `+`, `-`, `*`, `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=`, `=`, `not`

- **New bytecode VM** (`kl/vm.go`): Executes compiled functions with:
  - 22 opcodes including `OP_LOAD_CONST`, `OP_LOAD_LOCAL`, `OP_LOAD_UPVAL`, `OP_CALL`, `OP_TAIL_CALL`, `OP_MAKE_CLOSURE`, and arithmetic operations
  - Flat per-call local variable frames (eliminates alist environment chains)
  - Upvalue capture by value at closure creation time
  - Partial application support for under-application
  - Integration with existing trampoline-based control flow

- **Integration with existing evaluator** (`kl/eval.go`):
  - `defun` special form now compiles the body to bytecode and stores it in the symbol's `.function` slot
  - `apply()` dispatches to `vmApply()` for bytecode functions
  - Fallback to tree-walking interpreter for non-compiled forms

- **Bug fix** (`kl/primitives.go`): Fixed float comparison operators (`<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=`) to use `mustNumber()` instead of `mustInteger()`, which was truncating floats and causing incorrect results

- **Tests and benchmarks**:
  - Added comprehensive VM tests covering closures, trap-error, let-shadowing, currying, and tail calls
  - Added regression test for float comparisons
  - Added benchmark suite (`bench/bench.shen`) for tak, fib, nrev, and map-double
  - Documented performance results showing 6.6× speedup on tak and 60× on tail-recursive loops

## Implementation Details

- **Upvalue resolution**: Multi-level closures are supported through recursive upvalue discovery during compilation. Captured variables are loaded into the stack before `OP_MAKE_CLOSURE` and accessed via `OP_LOAD_UPVAL` in the inner function.

- **Tail-call handling**: Tail calls set `ControlFlowApply` and return to the existing trampoline. Self-tail calls (recursive calls in tail position) are optimized to jump back to `pc=0` with updated local slots, avoiding Go stack growth.

- **trap-error lowering**: `(trap-error body handler)` is compiled to `(try-catch (freeze body) handler)` at compile time, reusing the existing panic/recover primitive.

- **Global function lookup**: `OP_LOAD_GLOBAL` resolves symbols at runtime, ensuring redefined functions are always picked up without recompilation.

- **Constant pool**: All literals, nested bytecode functions, and symbols are stored in a per-function constant pool, indexed by the compiler.

items.title: feat(simd): opt-in adaptive-banded alignment mode (abPOA-style)
items.body:
## Summary

Adds an **opt-in, heuristic, abPOA-style adaptive-banded** alignment mode to `SimdEngine`. Banding computes only a per-node query-column window of the DP matrix, trading optimality for speed on near-identical short-read families (the target consumer: Global + convex, small UMI-style families of ~235 bp reads).

The default path is untouched and stays bit-exact with spoa: `SimdEngine::new` and `SisdEngine` behave exactly as before. Banding is reached only through the new `SimdEngine::banded(alignment_type, scoring, BandConfig)` constructor. A `SimdEngine::new` engine sets `band = None`, threads `None` through every dispatch site, and reproduces the full-matrix path byte-for-byte — the entire differential/parity suite (against the C++ spoa oracle) is unchanged.

Stacks conceptually on #11 (striped-backtrack), which is already merged into `main`; this PR targets `main`.

## Design

Full design and the two-pass adversarial-review trail are in `docs/design/2026-07-06-banded-poa-alignment-design.md`; the task-by-task plan is in `docs/design/2026-07-06-banded-poa-alignment-plan.md`.

Key mechanics:
- **Band geometry** (`band.rs`): a reverse-pass remaining-path length `R` gives a per-node query anchor `L − R`, unioned with predecessors' best-cell columns and widened by `w = base + round(frac·L)`. All geometry is `LANES`-independent, so bands are identical across ISAs.
- **Two-carry fill model**: the striped fills iterate only the in-band segments. The **diagonal** carry seeds from the predecessor buffer (it carries the match transition and must survive), while the **horizontal** gap-run carries close to `NEG_INF` at the band's left edge (ksw2-style). Vertical gap matrices (F/O) have no carry. Applied identically to linear/affine/convex via a shared `row_band` helper.
- **Saturating arithmetic**: banded fills use saturating `adds`/`subs` so an out-of-band `NEG_INF` sentinel can never wrap positive and win a `max`. int16 uses native saturating intrinsics; x86 int32 has no native saturating add/sub and is emulated (compare/blend with a sign-bit broadcast); NEON int32 is native.
- **Global endpoint**: read `H[sink, L]` or the sentinel (never a best-in-band scan, which would return a partial-query score), with a tier-correct sentinel normalization and a `max_score == NEG_INF` guard so the backtrack never steps into sentinel cells.

## Measured speedup (Apple M-series, Global/convex)

| point | build_family (end-to-end) | align_one (align-only) | cells computed |
|---|---|---|---|
| 6×235 | 2.50× | 3.26× | ~9.4× fewer |
| 10×235 | 2.70× | 3.31× | |
| 50×1000 | 5.03× | 6.29× | ~24× fewer |

`build_family` sits at the lower end of the cell-count ratio because fixed per-align overhead (graph mutation, scalar boundary init) does not shrink with the band; this is documented honestly in `benches/README.md`.

## Testing

- Per-cell exact-oracle gates at `beg_sn ≥ 1` for each fill (banded in-band cells equal the exact matrix), including reconvergent-graph fixtures that exercise the multi-predecessor diagonal seed.
- Property tests (`tests/banded_parity.rs`): `banded ≤ exact` across all 9 alignment-type × gap-mode combinations (sentinel-leak catch — zero violations), banded == exact on substitution-only families, and no-panic / in-band-traceback over random branching graphs.
- Full parity/differential suite unchanged (default path bit-exact); `clippy -D warnings` and `fmt` clean on aarch64 and x86_64.

## Scope / known limitations

- Banding is heuristic: it may miss alignments whose optimal path needs an indel wider than the band (pinned as an explicit contract test).
- Multi-sink Global true per-sink anchor is out of scope (documented Open in the design); the interim `NEG_INF` guard keeps such cases safe (exact-or-empty, never garbage).

## Suggested reading order

1. `docs/design/2026-07-06-banded-poa-alignment-design.md` — the spec + review trail.
2. `src/align/simd/band.rs` — band geometry (self-contained, unit-tested).
3. `src/align/simd/fill.rs` — the `row_band` helper + the two-carry banded clip (the correctness crux).
4. `src/align/simd/mod.rs` — `SimdEngine::banded` + the `align()` dispatch and `NEG_INF` guard.
5. `tests/banded_parity.rs` and `benches/poa.rs`.

items.title: Fix CUDA greedy ambiguity resolver correctness bug
items.body:
# Summary

This PR fixes correctness bugs in the CUDA greedy ambiguity resolver and re-enables the previously disabled CPU-vs-CUDA tests.

The core issue was that the CUDA resolver could silently return incorrect outputs on some workloads, often by removing no tracks at all and returning the full input unchanged.

## Problem (how it was observed)

During a synthetic GPU benchmark sweep, the CUDA resolver produced incorrect results in 8 of 9 configurations. The dominant failure mode was:

* `n_removed = 0`
* GPU output = all input candidates
* CPU and GPU selected-track sets did not match

## Root Cause

The CUDA resolver had four correctness bugs:

* `terminate_device` was allocated but never initialized to `0`, so reused device memory could start with `terminate=1` and cause the removal kernel to exit immediately.
* `scanned_block_offsets_buffer` was allocated but never passed through `setup()`, corrupting the prefix-sum metadata used to maintain sorted track order during iterative removals.
* `max_shared_device` was initialized with the wrong `cudaMemcpy` direction (`HostToDevice` instead of `DeviceToDevice`) even though the source pointer came from device memory.
* The outer loop copied `terminate` and `n_accepted` back to host asynchronously but did not synchronize before checking the loop condition, so host-side control flow could observe stale values.

_This PR applies the minimal correctness fixes necessary_

The extractor treated every argument-pass as an **escape** (untracked). So a stream handed to a consumer that owns it — `Archive(s)` where `Archive(Stream source)` disposes `source` — simply *vanished*, and a later touch of `s` was invisible. That's the use-after-handoff arm of `ownership-handoff-consume`, missed for that reason.

**Mechanism — a call-site release (the pool-`Return` pattern):** a call to a first-party **consumer** — a method whose *own body* disposes a by-value `IDisposable` parameter — is modelled as a **release of the matching argument at the call site**. A use of that argument *after* the call is then a use-after-release (**OWN002**), via the existing flow machinery. The argument is also exempted from the escape set so it stays tracked through the handoff.

- `ConsumeReleaseArg` + `DisposesLocal` — resolve the call's first-party target, and if its body disposes a by-value `IDisposable` parameter, return the matching argument's local name.
- The escape exemption is gated on the **same** `ConsumeReleaseArg` and on the bare `Consume(s);` statement form the flow pass actually lowers — so an argument is exempted **iff** it is also released (never a tracked-but-unreleased false leak), and only the arg bound to the disposed by-value param is exempted.

It is inter-procedural — the signal is the *callee's own body* — but there is **no cross-call signature table**, so a callee with no body (interface/abstract/extern) or that doesn't dispose the param yields nothing and the argument stays an ordinary escape. No dangling `call` op, no bridge crash.

> **Note — design pivot during review.** The first commit modelled the handoff as a `call` op resolved against the callee's signature in the OwnIR bridge. CI + Codex (P1) + CodeRabbit caught that it crashes on a consumer whose body the flow pass *skips* (`UnitOfWorkFlowSample`'s `ConsumeUnitOfWork`): the `call` op referenced an undeclared callee → unmapped `OWN040` → internal facts error (plus arg/param arity and an over-broad exemption). The call-site-release approach above **dissolves all of those by construction** (no `call` op → no OWN040/OWN041; exemption tied to the same body-inspection as the release → parameter-precise, no false leak; no callee-name key → no namespace collision). Same verdicts, crash-proof.

## The proof (benchmark, CI)

New fixture **`ownership-handoff-use`** (a *pure* use-after-handoff — no leak arm) is a **miss** before and a **catch (`OWN002`)** after: recall **8/10 → 9/11**. `ownership-handoff-consume` now fires **both** arms (`OWN001`+`OWN002`). Specificity stays **0 FP**, CI floor `--min-recall 9`.

**Validated locally (no .NET SDK):** the exact facts the extractor emits → `check_facts` → `OWN001`/`OWN002` (before) and silence (after), for *both* fixtures; `case.own` pins the logic (`test_corpus` **7/7**); the bridge machinery is intact (`test_ownir` **88/88**). items.title: [hipblaslt] adjust BufferOOB to 0xfffff000
items.body:
## Motivation
The current BufferOOB limit in the kernel writer assembly is statically capped at 2^{31} (0x80000000). When executing large GEMM operations (e.g., M=114278400), certain memory offsets exceed this signed 32-bit threshold. Since the hardware treats addresses beyond this restricted limit as out-of-bounds, valid write operations are silently dropped. This leads to incorrect computation results or "failed" status in hipBLASLt benchmarks
<!-- Explain the purpose of this PR and the goals it aims to achieve. -->

## Technical Details
While the hardware supports a full 32-bit range for buffer clamping, this change updates the BufferOOB value to 0xFFFFF000 instead of the theoretical maximum (0xFFFFFFFF).
This specific value is chosen to reserve a 4KB (12-bit) safety margin. This ensures that even when the hardware applies a maximum instruction offset (up to 4095) during memory access, the resulting address will not overflow the 32-bit boundary.
KernelWriterAssembly.py: Adjusted BufferOOB to 0xFFFFF000.

## Summary

- Fix checkpoint recovery to target CLIENT instances (where benchmarks run in fast mode)
- Add spot interruption detection for graceful shutdown with 2-minute AWS warning

## Changes

### Workflow Changes
- Changed terraform refresh target from `aws_spot_instance_request.arm64_runner` to `aws_instance.arm64_client`
- Changed terraform output from `arm64_instance_id` to `arm64_client_instance_id`

- Same changes for x86

### Spot Interruption Detection
- Added background goroutine that polls AWS metadata endpoint for spot interruption notices
- AWS provides 2-minute warning before termination at `http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/spot/instance-action`
- When interruption detected:
  - Logs the action type and scheduled termination time
  - Immediately saves checkpoint
  - Cancels benchmark context for clean shutdown
- Gracefully handles non-EC2 environments (silently stops monitoring)

## Why This Fix Works

In fast mode, benchmarks run on a single instance in LOCAL mode. The checkpoint is stored on the CLIENT instance at `/home/runner/work/benchmarks/benchmarks/results/checkpoint-{arch}.json`. The previous code incorrectly tried to recover from server instances.

The spot interruption detection allows the benchmark to save progress within seconds of receiving AWS termination notice, instead of waiting for GitHub Actions job timeout (up to 6 hours).

### 1. Why is this change necessary?

The original class detection logic in BenchExtension was incorrectly identifying fixture classes when loading group-specific data fixtures. It used end(get_declared_classes()) which could return the parent class (AbstractGroupAwareExtension) instead of the actual fixture class (e.g., IndividualPricingDataFixture). This caused group-specific fixtures to never be loaded, making it impossible to run benchmarks with features like Individual Pricing or Custom Pricing that require additional test data.

### 2. What does this change do, exactly?

This change fixes the class detection logic by:
Capturing all declared classes before requiring the fixture file
Capturing all declared classes after requiring the fixture file
Using array_diff() to find only the newly declared class
This ensures we always get the correct fixture class, not its parent

### 3. Describe each step to reproduce the issue or behaviour.

Create a benchmark test in custom/plugins/SwagCommercial/tests/performance/bench/Storefront/ with group attribute:
   ```php
   #[Bench\Groups(['individual-pricing'])]   public function bench_some_feature(): void { ... }
   ```
Create a group-specific data fixture at custom/plugins/SwagCommercial/tests/performance/bench/Common/IndividualPricing/DataFixture.php:

Run the benchmark with the group:
```

```
Expected: DataFixture should be loaded and test data created
Actual (before fix): DataFixture is not loaded because class detection returns AbstractGroupAwareExtension instead of DataFixture, causing is_subclass_of() check to fail

items.title: [2pt] Fixing incorrect benchmark results and Geocurves
items.body:
During testing and comparing ras2fim output units to benchmark data, we discovered some problems with geocurves. Many were not being created as expected.

Part of the evaluation of a unit is to use a new tool called `run_eval_bench_data.py`.  This is a WIP tool and requires a fair bit of hardcoding to be used at this time, but it is expected to evolve as time permits later.

The normal "alpha testing" evaluation of a unit is to run the `run_test_cases.py` against a unit, then run `run_eval_bench_data.py` to see metrics and agreement rasters.

**Note: This release does require a ras2fim Conda environment reload**

### Additions  

- `tools\run_eval_bench_data.py`: as described above.

### File Renamed
- Was: `tools\run_unit_benchmark_tests.py`,  Now: `run_test_cases.py`: This is the same name as used in the FIM product for this functionality and helps minimize confusion.

### Changes  

- `environment.yml`: Adding seaborn used for plots and updated a few other packages
- `src`
    - `conflate_hecras_to_nwm.py`: Linting fixes
    - `create_geocurves.py`: A wide number of changes to fix the bug listed above. It also has significantly upgraded logging.
    - `create_shapes_from_hecras.py`: Added a note about an import fix required later. See Issue [323](https://github.com/NOAA-OWP/ras2fim/issues/323) Change logic of filtering out models and key model files.
- `tools`
     - `ras2inundation.py`: A validation fix.
    - `run_test_cases.py`: (renamed as mentioned above): Some linting updates and some debugging cleanup
    - `acquire_and_preprocess_3dep_dems.py`: A small fix to disable the levee system in this script. The levee system is not fully operational system wide.

### Testing

A very wide array of testing was done with small set models, plus full units (all models).  

To test:
- Update your conda environment.
- Ensure you have or build a full set of models for a HUC.
- Load the latest eval_PROD_metrics.csv from S3. If you already have on downloaded, remember that the eval system will overwrite records in the metrics file that match the unit_name and unit_version.  ie) 12090301_2277_ble_240519.
- Run the `tools\run_test_cases.py`. Watch the notes and args as this is stable tool but some args have never been tested. It is encouraged to use the defaults args and pathing. This will give you metrics files and agreement files.
- Run the `tools\run_eval_bench_data.py`. It is a very new tool and is in rough prototype form. You will need to change some hardcoded values in order to use at this time, but it is very valuable to comparing results from V1 to V2 or any version of a unit.

In this PR, we address the incorrect performance results on the benchmarks for fetchPage and fetchResource caused by the high variance of network latency. To achieve more reliable performance data, we mock the network calls of fetchResource in the benchmarks as we did with the tests.

Changes:

Vitest Benchmarks with Mocked Network Calls
- Updated benchmarks in page_fetching.bench.ts and resource.bench.ts to mock system calls, which removes network latency variance.
- Created a mocked SuiClient using vi.fn() to simulate responses for the fetchPage and fetchResource functions.

items.body:
This PR adds the ability for admins to assign a task to a specific worker via a special header(`X-WORKER-ID`) when creating a task from a flow.

This is mainly needed for debugging servers where many workers are connected and you need to track why some worker, for example, produces incorrect results.

This will also be used in a new benchmark, which will add the ability to work with an instance where there are many workers.

items.title: Implement "into SSA" and "out of SSA" transformations
items.body:
This pull request addresses the task from Lesson 6 by implementing support for converting between SSA form and non-SSA form.

To convert **to** SSA form, I followed the two-step pseudo-code introduced in class. Arguments of Φ-nodes that are undefined along a path are suffixed with `.undef`.  
To convert **out** of SSA form, I introduce copy (id) instructions along each predecessor path that contributes a different symbol.

### Challenges and Insights

Converting Φ-nodes to id instructions can result in id instructions that rename each other, potentially leading to undefined variables. To mitigate this, I represented these instructions as a graph and detected cycles. Any id instructions forming a cycle are excluded from the final output. However, this approach might inadvertently remove essential id instructions. The exact conditions under which circular id instructions are necessary remain unclear and require further investigation.

To test the correctness of the conversion, I ran the core benchmarks. Three programs produced incorrect results due to the removal of necessary id instructions. 😢

For other programs, the overhead after the round trip is shown below:

items.title: Sparse trie
items.body:
## Faster root hash

This pr introduces option to use sparse merkle trie implementation for the root hash calculation.

This implementation fetches relevant pieces of the trie into memory making subsequent root hash calculations faster.

On my PC reference implementation takes about 150ms to calculate hash and the new one when everything is prefetched around 5ms. 

Fetching proof for data for one uncached account takes about 0.25ms.

There are things to improve in implementation itself but the basic interface for the integration into the builder will be the same. 


## debug-bench-machine

This PR also redoes debug-bench-machine.  Now you need to stop reth node and provide external rpc for it to work. 

The reason is that reth has trie only for the last block. Previous implementation used last block to generate changes and it applied that changes to the trie after the last block. Trie would already have these changes but default reth root hash does not care about that discrepancy and it would evaluate anyway, this was used as a hack to benchmark trie even though it would give incorrect results. 

Sparse trie implemenation would not work like that because it would detect errors such as removing key that was already removed from the trie. 

The benefit of this is that we can actually check correctness of the root hash on historical block.
